messages.subject: Highlighting other languages gives error if a comment (`#`) is used when knitting a LaTeX doc
messages.subject_clean: Highlighting other languages gives error if a comment (`#`) is used when knitting a LaTeX doc
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Not sure if this is a local problem or a reproducible one but if I write a chunk in bash or python and include a comment, LaTeX will give an error related to the highlighting app.

The original example code parses fine:

\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
Syntax highlighting also works for other languages in the \LaTeX{} or HTML output, if Highlight has been installed (and is in PATH).
<<hi-python, engine='python'>>=
x = 'hello, python world!'
print x
print x.split(' ')
@
\end{document}

But given a comment

\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
Syntax highlighting also works for other languages in the \LaTeX{} or HTML output, if Highlight has been installed (and is in PATH).
<<hi-python, engine='python'>>=
# comment
x = 'hello, python world!'
print x
print x.split(' ')
@
\end{document}

I get:

! Undefined control sequence.

l.60 \hlstd{}\hlslc

{\#\ comment}\hspace*{\fill}\\

[1] (./test.aux) )

Same goes for bash, haven't tried other languages, but I assume that any language which uses # to indicate comment will give and error.

Any idea why this is happening?

Roey

Is there a cleaner/safer way?

flag, getOption('knitr.in.progress') (TRUE if knitting is in progress,

Thanks for the information!

It is a bit obscure behavior, but the use case is specific.  Basically, if the code is being knit into a report, it should just report the key information, if it is run separately, it prints more verbose output (a bit like an automatic verbose flag).

Certainly I could add a couple lines of code so that everything runs, but only the bit I want is actually printed in the report, but that is a bit of extra code everytime versus a simple hack: verbose = isTRUE(getOption('knit.in.progress')).

It only needs to be "reliable" in the sense that I can specify whatever knitr options I want without fear that my check gets broken in this specific case.

Anyway, much appreciate the help!

Josh

messages.body_plain:
Just bumped to a different use case that needs to detect whether knit
is running or not, e.g.

> BiocStyle::latex
function (..., width = 90, short.fignames = FALSE, fig.path,
    error = FALSE, use.unsrturl = TRUE)
{
    options(..., width = width)
    cat(sprintf("\\RequirePackage{%s}\n\n", sub(".sty$", "",
        .bioconductor.sty)))
    if (use.unsrturl) {
        bst <- file.path(system.file(package = "BiocStyle", "resources",
            "latex"), "unsrturl")
        cat(sprintf("\\AtBeginDocument{\\bibliographystyle{%s}}\n",
            bst))
    }
    setPrefix = function(x) {
        cat(sprintf("\\renewcommand{\\prefix}[1]{%s#1}", x))
    }
    fs = sapply(sys.calls(), function(x) as.character(x)[1])
    id = pmatch("knit", fs, nomatch = 0)
    if (id > 0 && exists("opts_chunk")) {
        if (missing(fig.path)) {
            fig.path = knitr::opts_chunk$get("fig.path", default = TRUE)
        }
        if (isTRUE(short.fignames))
            setPrefix(fig.path)
        knitr::opts_knit$set(latex.options.color = "usenames,dvipsnames")
        knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = fig.path, error = error)
    }
    else {
        if (isTRUE(short.fignames))
            setPrefix("\\jobname-")
    }
}
<environment: namespace:BiocStyle>

Quite a hack that would be better done with a knitr::is_knitting() function.

/Henrik

Dan: Sorry, I forgot to update NEWS this time since I always update
NEWS.md (https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS.md).

In general, package authors are not expected to use hard-coded figure
filenames in their vignettes. I'm aware that some authors have code
like this in their vignettes:

<<foo, include=FALSE>>=
plot(1:10)
@
\begin{figure}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics{figure/foo}
\caption{A figure foo.}
\end{center}
\end{figure}

Since knitr 1.7, the filename will be foo-1 instead of foo. I need to
see some convincing use cases on why the LaTeX code with hard-coded
figure filenames is necessary, because it is entirely possible and
even more compact to write

<<foo, fig.cap="A figure foo.", fig.align="center">>=
plot(1:10)
@

which automatically generates the appropriate LaTeX code with a single
R code chunk, and authors will never need to consider the filenames.

This is rather hidden as a minor change, but it broke quite a few of my reports on recompiling.

..for R Markdown v2 documents, if the inline R output is formatted using the scientific notation, the output must be put in a math environment, e.g. $`r 2e10`$...

I checked and the p-values computed by dcov.test are consistent and correct given the replicates that are returned by dcov.test. However, the numerical values of the replicates for this particular random number seed seem to be wrong. Strangely, by generating just one random number before the test, I can obtain the p-value 0.005 and the replicates look fine. Another fact is that the inconsistency is not there if I take the first 30 or first 60 rows of the data frame instead of all of it.

The reason that the p-value here is decreasing with the number of replicates is that the observed value of the test statistic is very far from the null sampling distribution. The null sampling distribution should be invariant if we generate all permutations, so it should be approximately invariant if we generate 199. (The p-values decreasing with number of replicates is similar to what would happen if the null distribution is standard normal while the observed test statistic is say, 100.)  On the other hand, what happens with this data running in knitr is that unless the random number seed is set or updated in code appearing before the test, the replicates generated in the full example are simply wrong - not even close to the null distribution we get with a simple replicate() version of the test.

So I have one concrete example of apparently corrupted data in the replicates, which it seems must be internal to energy as some type of incompatibility with knitr, but so far I have been unable to come up with a single other example in which the sampling distribution of the replicates generated differs in knitr from the result when running the same code at the console.

Thanks to everyone that took time to look into this. It will be hard to find the cause of this issue but I am working on it.

Good point. However, in that case, the random seed was introduced by
the user in the first place, instead of knitr. What knitr did was
simply saving the random seed triggered by user's code. Maria's guess
was knitr touched the random seed somewhere internally, and I could
not think of any place in which knitr could possibly touch it by
itself. Some packages, however, do change the state of RNG, e.g.
ggplot2 uses runif() to decide whether to print a start-up message:

missing GetRNGstate() in my code has different consequences in knitr vs console:

Checking the source, in RNG.c the RNG_Init function should be called when
there is no .Random.seed, but without GetRNGstate() it might not be called:

static void Randomize(RNGtype kind)
{
/* Only called by  GetRNGstate() when there is no .Random.seed */
    RNG_Init(kind, TimeToSeed());
}

RNG_Init does not happen.

  Rprintf("%f\\n", x);
  return R_NilValue;

  double x = unif_rand();
  PutRNGstate();
  Rprintf("%f\\n", x);
  return R_NilValue;
